turn.subject: solution
turn.user_message: Yes, that’s exactly it. Show me how to fix it.

text: Here’s what the fix is made of. It has five parts.
None of them needs a new hospital system on day one. They sit on top of how you work today.
chat.pointer: Each part opens to show what’s in it. Pick the one you want to start with.
chat.note: Five parts, one aim: put the evening to work.
prompts: Which part saves the most time?
Do we need to hire anyone?

blocks.title: What the fix is made of
blocks.deck: Five parts. Open any one to see what’s in it.

items.title: Automatic paperwork
items.text: What the software does, so nobody does the work twice.
items.more: Other hospitals saved 6 to 8 hours for each patient. Not yet measured here.
more_points: Starts the going-home papers when a doctor first mentions it, even on the evening round.
Keeps a record of every test, medicine and procedure from the day the patient arrives.
Keeps the bill up to date all the time, so it is ready the moment the doctor signs.
Works out which unused medicines go back to pharmacy, so nurses don’t count them first.
Sends a first bill to the insurance company the evening before.
Lets the doctor check and sign on a phone or tablet during the morning round.

items.title: Changes on the wards
items.text: What each team does differently, step by step.
more_points: The steps stay the same. They start earlier and run side by side.
Staff approve what the software prepares, instead of writing it by hand.
Your IT team connects the software to your hospital systems, reports and notes.
Pharmacy, diet, housekeeping and transport teams are told exactly when they’re needed.
If one team does both discharges and admissions, the two jobs are split or run together.
The bed desk writes down when each bed is given out and when the next patient arrives.

items.title: People who must agree
items.text: Who has to say yes, and what each is asked to do.
items.more: Each team is told the software takes work off them. It does not replace them.
more_points: Doctors: start the going-home papers in the evening, then sign on a phone next morning.
Nurses: check what the software writes down from the doctors’ notes.
Billing and the insurance desk: check bills that are already made.
IT, lab and scan teams: keep reports up to date in the system.
Admissions, housekeeping, the dietitian and the ward manager: act when the software tells them.
Head of Operations: approves the new order of steps. Without this, the change won’t last.

items.title: Who is in charge
items.text: Whether you need someone new to run this.
more_points: Most teams only record and approve a little more in the system.
A Discharge Manager runs the whole process and works with the other departments. About ₹4 to 4.5 lakh a year.
Discharge Executives look after each patient going home. About ₹3 to 3.5 lakh a year each.
How many executives you need depends on your busiest hours. We work that out together.

items.title: How we’ll know it worked
items.text: The few numbers we will watch, week by week.
more_points: Time from the doctor saying ‘go home’ to the patient leaving.
How many patients paying themselves leave by 10 AM (11 AM at the latest), and insured patients by 1 PM.
How many going-home decisions start on the evening round.
How long insurance approval takes, in the evening and in the morning.
How long a bed takes to be ready for the next patient.
Whether every family hears about diet, medicines and follow-up before leaving.
